title: Results that are still there when you return
kicker: Five provider-neutral proposals for Claude and Codex
brief: Replace perishable agent-server links with a result contract: after an agent finishes, a recipient opening the chat days later should get an immediately useful, honest result without reviving a terminal or discovering which port once hosted it.
defaultWhy: The Review Resolver wins at 94/100 because it makes one durable Result card responsible for resolving to the best available representation, while requiring a static fallback for every live experience. It is a product protocol rather than merely another place to host a server.
decisionHinge: This recommendation assumes Claude and Codex can agree to implement a small shared result manifest. If cross-provider coordination is unavailable, shift the 10% agent-cost weight to immediate delivery: V1’s attached Review Bundle becomes the strongest independent default (90/100).
invariants: Use the same return-later fixture: a user opens a completed chat three days after the agent process has stopped.
Each proposal retains a report, a visual capture, source/revision provenance, and a clearly marked live-versus-static state.
A raw localhost port or agent-shell process is never the sole review destination.
Retention, access, and deletion are visible to the user rather than implied by an agent’s lifetime.
boundary: This is a product-concept gallery, not an implementation or a proof of either provider’s current capabilities. The interactive diagrams model the return-later contract; scores are reasoned design judgments, not operational measurements.

requirements.name: Reliable return later
requirements.why: The stated failure is that a result is dead by the time its recipient opens the chat again.
requirements.passCondition: A result opened three days later remains useful without the original agent process or its ephemeral port.

anchors.1: A raw localhost or task URL fails when the agent session ends.
anchors.3: A result usually survives but has an unhandled expiry, device, or process dependency.
anchors.5: The result is retained by contract and its non-live fallback also opens independently.

requirements.name: Instant inspection
requirements.why: A review link should feel like opening an attachment, not resuming an operations task.
requirements.passCondition: The recipient sees a useful rendered result immediately after activating the chat’s review card.

anchors.1: The recipient must find a terminal, revive a server, or diagnose a broken URL.
anchors.3: A progress state appears before a usable result, but recovery is automatic.
anchors.5: A useful static result is visible at once, with no recovery action.

requirements.name: Truthful interactive fidelity
requirements.why: For an app or canvas, a screenshot alone can conceal the behavior the user needs to judge.
requirements.passCondition: When interaction is the result, the approach preserves a truthful way to exercise it or clearly labels the retained evidence as static.

anchors.1: The result silently degrades into an unlabelled or misleading picture.
anchors.3: A recording or reconstruction survives but cannot exercise the original interaction.
anchors.5: A live version remains available when relevant and the static evidence is a clear fallback.

requirements.name: User control and privacy
requirements.why: Results may contain local code, data, or work-in-progress and should remain understandable and recoverable by their owner.
requirements.passCondition: The recipient can identify where the bytes live, how long they remain, and how to export or remove them.

anchors.1: Retention, access, or deletion is opaque.
anchors.3: The storage is understandable but controlled mainly by a provider or a fragile machine state.
anchors.5: Retention, access, export, and deletion are explicit user-facing controls.

requirements.name: Low agent-operational burden
requirements.why: Reliability should be a product default, not something a user must remember to request on every task.
requirements.passCondition: An ordinary result is published and health-checked automatically with minimal per-task setup.

anchors.1: Every task needs bespoke ports, manual deployment, or cleanup.
anchors.3: The provider automates some lifecycle work but special cases are routine.
anchors.5: The durable result is the normal completion path and lifecycle is automatic.

hardGates.name: No raw ephemeral server link as the only result
hardGates.why: A bare task-owned port has no retention contract and cannot meet the return-later promise.

hardGates.name: A visible, labelled fallback exists for every live result
hardGates.why: A user should still get a useful report, recording, or explanation if a live runtime cannot be restored.

variants.name: Attached Review Bundle
variants.thesis: Make a self-contained result attachment—not a server URL—the default thing an agent leaves in chat.
variants.bestWhen: The output is a report, HTML prototype, images, diff, or short interaction capture; maximum reliability and a one-click result matter more than a running backend.
variants.losesWhen: The essential result depends on a real multi-user service, writable state, hardware, or a large dataset that cannot sensibly be packaged.

decisions.label: Canonical object
decisions.value: A content-addressed bundle: rendered HTML, media, source revision, and a small result manifest.

decisions.label: Chat surface
decisions.value: A first-class Result card opens the bundle inside the provider, with download/export rather than a raw port.

decisions.label: Live boundary
decisions.value: Interactive behavior is captured as an annotated replay or video when the actual runtime cannot travel in the bundle.

proof: The direct control switches from completion to the three-days-later state without relying on a server.
This concept is static evidence by design; it does not prove a live backend can be preserved.

steps.label: Agent attaches the result
steps.caption: The canonical deliverable is an immutable Review Bundle already resident in the conversation.

steps.label: Return after the server died
steps.caption: The attachment still opens because no task-owned server was part of the basic path.

return.evidence: The bundle is independent of the original task process once persisted.

instant.evidence: Opening an attachment can render immediately in the chat client.

fidelity.evidence: A replay is honest but cannot retain arbitrary server-side interaction.

ownership.evidence: Conversation-owned retention and export can be explicit, but provider retention remains a policy dependency.

agent_cost.evidence: Packaging can be the ordinary completion operation rather than task-specific server management.

stable-reference.evidence: The chat card resolves to a stored bundle ID, never to a one-off port.

honest-fallback.evidence: The review card exposes a retained static or recorded fallback instead of silently failing.

variants.name: User-owned Result Library
variants.thesis: Give each desktop client a durable, browsable shelf of every finished result, stored locally and indexed by task.
variants.bestWhen: The user primarily returns on the same personal machine and values private local artifacts, search, and durable offline access.
variants.losesWhen: Results must open from another device or be shared with people who lack that local library; syncing then becomes a separate product commitment.

decisions.label: Canonical object
decisions.value: A local content-addressed result directory, plus a task/result index and retention controls.

decisions.label: Chat surface
decisions.value: The chat card deep-links to a native review pane; it does not expose localhost routing.

decisions.label: Recovery
decisions.value: A finished result is independent of the task terminal and can be searched, exported, or pinned from the Library.

proof: The alternate state models the desktop client reading stored bytes after the agent’s task has disappeared.
Cross-device sync is deliberately outside this proposal’s stop line.

steps.label: Result enters the shelf
steps.caption: Completion persists a local package and registers its task and revision metadata.

steps.label: Open it later
steps.caption: The app serves the stored result directly rather than asking an old dev server to answer.

return.evidence: Local persisted content survives agent/task lifetime while the device and library are retained.

instant.evidence: The desktop can open the saved artifact without network or runtime startup.

fidelity.evidence: It preserves static captures and client-side prototypes; arbitrary services remain out of scope.

ownership.evidence: The user controls the files, retention, export, and deletion on their device.

agent_cost.evidence: The client needs indexing, storage management, and eventually sync, though individual agents need little setup.

stable-reference.evidence: The card resolves to a durable library record, with an exportable bundle as the fallback.

honest-fallback.evidence: The review card exposes a retained static or recorded fallback instead of silently failing.

variants.name: Immutable Review Site
variants.thesis: Publish each completed result to a stable, authenticated web address backed by immutable static hosting.
variants.bestWhen: The result should open from any device, be shareable, and consist largely of a built app, report, media, or read-only browser interaction.
variants.losesWhen: Sensitive local data cannot leave the machine or the cost/governance of hosted retention is unacceptable.

decisions.label: Canonical object
decisions.value: An immutable build addressed by result ID and source revision, with a retention policy shown in the card.

decisions.label: Chat surface
decisions.value: A persistent authenticated URL points to a static deployment—not the agent’s Vite or notebook port.

decisions.label: Live boundary
decisions.value: Read-only browser behavior can be built into the site; server-dependent behavior links to an honest captured fallback.

proof: The later state represents an immutable deployment that has no relationship to the agent’s finished shell.
Actual ACL, retention period, and cloud cost are product-policy questions, not proven by this concept.

steps.label: Publish the review build
steps.caption: The agent publishes a signed immutable build, then the card records its stable result ID.

steps.label: Open from a later chat
steps.caption: The hosted static build remains directly available after the originating runtime ends.

return.evidence: Immutable object storage/CDN retention can be contractual and decoupled from the agent process.

instant.evidence: Static hosting can serve a useful initial document immediately.

fidelity.evidence: Read-only browser apps and static interactions survive; an arbitrary backend still needs a separate strategy.

ownership.evidence: Access can be controlled, but the bytes and retention live in provider-operated infrastructure.

agent_cost.evidence: A standard publish pipeline is automatable, with hosting governance as the fixed operational cost.

stable-reference.evidence: The review ID maps to a retained immutable object, not to a port on the task host.

honest-fallback.evidence: The review card exposes a retained static or recorded fallback instead of silently failing.

variants.name: Hibernating Preview Capsule
variants.thesis: Preserve the actual live preview in a snapshotable capsule that sleeps when idle and wakes when its result URL is opened.
variants.bestWhen: The behavior itself matters—e.g. a real API, data transform, integrated app, or richer test fixture—and a static reconstruction would be misleading.
variants.losesWhen: The user expects true instant opening, the environment is difficult to snapshot securely, or the cost of keeping restorable runtimes is unjustified.

decisions.label: Canonical object
decisions.value: A signed runtime image plus data snapshot, static cover page, health contract, and expiry policy.

decisions.label: Chat surface
decisions.value: The review card first shows a retained cover and status; it wakes the capsule automatically rather than surfacing a dead port.

decisions.label: Fallback
decisions.value: When wake fails or the lease has expired, the same card opens the bundled report, captures, logs, and provenance.

proof: The toggle models automatic restoration after the original agent service has ended.
Startup latency, secret stripping, and real snapshot restoration need operational acceptance testing before this could be a promise.

steps.label: Capsule hibernates
steps.caption: The result card keeps a static cover while idle, so a completed task no longer owns an exposed port.

steps.label: Return and wake
steps.caption: Opening the card restores the snapshot; the fallback remains available if the wake cannot complete.

return.evidence: A retained image can be restored, but its lease and dependencies introduce more failure modes than a static object.

instant.evidence: The cover is immediate, but faithful live interaction requires a wake delay.

fidelity.evidence: The actual application and service state can remain exerciseable rather than merely recorded.

ownership.evidence: A user-visible lease and export can give control, though a runtime platform still operates the capsule.

agent_cost.evidence: Snapshotting, safe wake-up, health checks, and expiry handling are substantial platform operations.

stable-reference.evidence: The capsule URL resolves through a retained result record and always has a static cover/fallback.

honest-fallback.evidence: The review card exposes a retained static or recorded fallback instead of silently failing.

variants.name: Review Resolver Contract
variants.thesis: Standardize one Result card and manifest that selects the best surviving representation—live, hosted, local, or static—then visibly falls back.
variants.bestWhen: A person uses more than one agent or device and wants every result link to behave predictably, even though the underlying output types vary widely.
variants.losesWhen: The providers cannot coordinate on a portable manifest or the platform cannot afford to retain even a minimal static fallback for every completed result.

decisions.label: Canonical object
decisions.value: A portable `review.json` references immutable static evidence, optional live endpoints, provenance, access, and retention policy.

decisions.label: Chat surface
decisions.value: Every agent emits one Result card. The client resolves it in order: live healthy preview → immutable site/local copy → self-contained bundle.

decisions.label: Reliability promise
decisions.value: The user never receives a naked port; health checks and automatic fallback are owned by the resolver, not improvised by each agent.

proof: The direct control demonstrates the core state change: a live endpoint can disappear while the card still resolves to a retained result.
The cross-provider manifest and resolver would require a shared product/API decision; this gallery does not claim either exists today.

steps.label: Use the highest-fidelity view
steps.caption: When a live preview is healthy, the Result card can open it while preserving the manifest and fallback choices.

steps.label: Resolve after live loss
steps.caption: When the agent runtime disappears, the same card automatically picks the immutable/static representation and labels why.

return.evidence: The resolver makes retained fallback part of the contract rather than relying on a single runtime destination.

instant.evidence: It can resolve directly to a ready static representation while a higher-fidelity option is unavailable or waking.

fidelity.evidence: It may choose a verified live view when available but never hides the static evidence path.

ownership.evidence: The manifest can expose storage, policy, export, and deletion across destinations, though some bytes remain provider-hosted.

agent_cost.evidence: The shared resolver is a meaningful platform investment, but it eliminates per-agent lifecycle improvisation afterward.

stable-reference.evidence: The durable Result card resolves a manifest, which must contain static evidence even when it also offers live URLs.

honest-fallback.evidence: The review card exposes a retained static or recorded fallback instead of silently failing.
